title: Bea and Sprocket's Echo Adventure
markdown:
In a little bakery that smelled of cinnamon and dreams, lived Bea. She was a baker’s daughter, which meant her nose was usually dusted with flour and her pockets always held cookie crumbs. She had a laugh like little bells jingling. Right there with her, practically her best friend, was Sprocket. Not just any mouse: he lived in the cozy cobwebby attic, a place that smelled of old paper and forgotten adventures. He was braver and smarter than a whole army of library mice. His whiskers twitched at everything. His tiny paws were ready even for a quick dash to snag a fallen sprinkle. Together they built imaginary bread castles that stretched to the ceiling and shared secrets whispered between flour sacks. On rainy days the bakery felt like a ship, warm and creaking, and they were the crew.

One afternoon the sky decided to cry. Pitter-patter. Drip-drop. A proper rainy day, the kind that asked for cocoa. Bea was helping Papa ready a batch of sparkly-sugar cookies when the dough timer — round, red, a bit wobbly, as if a giggly inventor had made it — began to behave.

Tick-tock-tick-tock. Then faster. It wobbled off the counter with a boing, another boing, a boing-whoosh past Bea’s nose, a tiny round race car on the warm boards.

“Oh no!” Sprocket squeaked from a sugar sack, eyes like black buttons. He had been napping. The whoosh un-napped him.

The timer did not stop. It bounced under a dresser that had not moved since anyone could remember. Clang against the wall. Then it vanished behind a loose stone Bea had never noticed. The wall seemed to swallow it.

“Where did it go?” Bea’s brow furrowed. Flour stayed on her nose.

Sprocket scurried down, whiskers quivering. “Somewhere new. And I heard it. Echoey.”

She peered at the stone: grey, crumbly, ordinary. Sprocket was rarely wrong about sounds. He had the best ears in the bakery, possibly the town. She tapped. Thump. Harder, ear close. Thump… thump… a faint echo, a whisper coming back.

“Echoes? Like a cave? Or a long empty hall?”

“Exactly!” His tail flicked. “They bounce. Especially in tight spots. Sound-balloons.”

Her eyes lit with that baker’s-daughter sparkle that means an adventure has clocked in. “So if we listen carefully, we can follow the tock.”

She pushed the stone. It grumbled like an old man waking and moved enough to show a dark narrow opening. Old secrets, damp earth, a rumour of forgotten cookies. “Ready, Sprocket?”

“Ready as I’ll ever be.” He sniffed, vibrating.

Tick-tock… faintly, from the dark.

“There it goes.” She squeezed into a passage tighter than it looked. Sprocket scampered beside her, feet almost silent. A draft whooshed, carrying a strange sweet smell, like flowers someone had misplaced. Every sound bounced, as if the passage wanted a turn.

“Hellooo,” she called softly.

Hellooo… hellooo… a playful ghost of her voice.

“A giant whispering game,” Sprocket said. “The passage wants to play.”

They followed the tick-tock and listened to how the echoes changed. In some stretches the tocks came back super fast, bumping into each other — tock-tock-tock — which meant the passage was narrow, a very snug hug from the walls. In other spots the echoes took their time, lazily drifting — tock… tock… — which meant the space was wider. A secret map made of sound. Bea imagined the tocks as little glowing dots, guiding them deeper.

The floor sloped. Dust puffed. Once Sprocket sneezed and the sneeze came back three times, which made them both giggle and then shush themselves, because giggling also bounced. But the timer’s beat was still there, stubborn as a good recipe.

The passage narrowed until her shoulders brushed both sides. Therefore they turned sideways and let Sprocket go first, a scout with better whiskers than maps. But a drip from the ceiling made a false tock, and for a moment they followed water. Therefore she stopped, held her breath, and waited for the red timer’s true stubborn beat. It came from ahead and a little down. She put her palm on the stone. It was cooler than the bakery, and a little wet, and it hummed when the timer tocked, as if the wall liked the game too.

“It’s getting louder.” Her heart drummed a happy solo. The way opened. She could walk without scraping. The tick-tock was determined now, a welcome. They rounded a bend.

A small round room, not dark at all. Soft glowing moss clung to the walls, green and blue. A secret cavern under the bakery. In the middle, wobbling merrily on a smooth grey stone, sat the dough timer, pleased with itself, as if it had always meant to find the best bounces.

“You found it!” Bea scooped it up. Warm, as if it had soaked in the moss-light.

Sprocket pirouetted. “A secret fairy party. Or a gnome disco.”

They looked around the glowing chamber, marvelling. The timer’s tick-tock filled the small space with a happy energetic rhythm, a tiny heart in a secret room. It had not been lost, not really. It had found a sparkling place to wait and listen to the best bounces. Bea imagined the moss singing a soft glowing song to the red metal. Sprocket counted the echoes on his claws and lost count, which he considered scientific.

Bea hugged the timer. “Well, little timer, you certainly know how to make an entrance. And an exit. You almost gave us a run for our money.”

Sprocket puffed his little chest. “We followed the echoes. That was clever. And you, Bea, for figuring it out.”

They turned back toward the passage. The glowing moss faded as they re-entered the dim tunnel. Bea carried the timer carefully. Sprocket trotted by her side. Their footsteps became ordinary footsteps, no longer bouncing so wildly. They pushed the loose stone and blinked as the familiar warm light of the bakery spilled over them — yeast, sugar, home.

Papa looked up from kneading, flour on his apron like a friendly snow. “Look who’s back. And with the timer. A good explore?”

Bea grinned. “A secret passage. Echoes. A glowing room.”

Sprocket nodded, mouse-modest and very brave.

Rain still greyed the windows. Inside, the timer sat on the counter and behaved, mostly. Bea set it where it could see the stone, just in case it got ideas. Sprocket claimed the sugar sack again. The next batch of cookies would rise on time, and the passage, behind its ordinary grey, kept the moss and the game for another rainy afternoon.
